name: Muon optimizer for hidden 2-D matrices (AdamW kept for embeddings/head/1-D params)
current: Single AdamW over all params (lr 2e-3, wd 0.1 on >=2D incl. tied embedding), betas default (0.9,0.999).
proposal: Hybrid optimizer: Muon (SGD-Nesterov momentum 0.95 -> Newton-Schulz-5 orthogonalization) for all 2-D weights inside Blocks (q/k/v, attn proj, MLP fc/proj). AdamW (betas 0.9,0.95) for the tied token embedding/lm_head, position embedding, LayerNorm params and biases. Muon effective lr ≈ 0.02 (or Moonlight-style 0.2*sqrt(max(m,n)) RMS matching with the AdamW lr).
mechanism: Orthogonalizing the momentum equalizes singular values of each update, amplifying rare directions that AdamW's update under-weights. That gives more loss decrease per token. This matters here because the token budget is fixed and the model is still improving at the end of training.

evidence.source: Keller Jordan, 'Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks' (blog)
evidence.finding: Muon sets the NanoGPT/FineWeb speedrun records, a 1.35x speedup over AdamW at 124M. It is applied only to hidden 2-D params; embeddings, head and scalars stay on AdamW. NS coefficients (3.4445,-4.7750,2.0315), 5 steps, Nesterov momentum.

evidence.source: Liu et al., 'Muon is Scalable for LLM Training' (Moonlight)
evidence.finding: With weight decay and per-parameter update-RMS matching to AdamW, Muon is ~2x more sample-efficient than AdamW in compute-optimal scaling-law runs.

expected_effect: Largest single expected gain: roughly −0.05 to −0.12 nats of val loss at an equal token budget (speedrun evidence ≈ AdamW needing 1.35x+ more tokens).
applicability: The evidence is from 124M-and-up models on FineWeb, the same data family as here. Hidden matrices are small (256×256 and 256×1024), so NS-5 in fp32 costs <2% of step time. The non-embedding part is only 4.8M params, so the gain may be smaller than at 124M because AdamW still handles the dominant embedding table.
risks: The training loop overwrites every group's lr, so the Muon lr must be derived via a per-group multiplier. Too high a Muon lr with no QK-norm can cause logit growth. In fp32, NS needs normalization by the Frobenius norm first.
implementation: In build_optimizer: hidden=[p for n,p in model.named_parameters() if p.dim()==2 and 'blocks.' in n]; others split into decay/no-decay AdamW groups. Write a class Hybrid(torch.optim.Optimizer) holding groups tagged {'muon':True,'lr_mult':10}. In step(), for Muon groups: buf=state.momentum_buffer; buf.mul_(0.95).add_(g); g=g.add(buf,alpha=0.95) (nesterov); X=g/(g.norm()+1e-7); transpose if rows>cols; for _ in 5: A=X@X.T; B=b*A+c*A@A; X=a*X+B@X; scale by max(1,rows/cols)**0.5; p.mul_(1-lr*wd); p.add_(X,alpha=-lr*lr_mult). For AdamW groups, run a standard Adam update inline (or hold an internal torch AdamW and copy lr). Keep lr=2e-3 for the Adam parts, Muon lr = 0.02 (lr_mult 10); sweep lr_mult 5–20.

name: RoPE + QK-norm in a fused multi-head attention (drop learned absolute positions)
current: Learned absolute position table added to token embeddings. Per-head Python loop of separate Linears. Manual softmax path in eval (a different code path from training). No normalization of q/k.
proposal: Single qkv Linear(n_embd,3*n_embd) reshaped to (B,H,T,hd). Apply RMSNorm (or F.rms_norm) to q and k per head, then rotary embeddings (base 10000) to q,k, then F.scaled_dot_product_attention(is_causal=True) in both train and eval. Remove position_embedding_table and pos_emb add.
mechanism: RoPE injects relative position into q·k, which is a better inductive bias than an additive learned table at T=128 and frees the residual stream. QK-norm bounds attention logits, which stabilizes training and tolerates higher LR (it pairs well with Muon). Fusing the heads removes 3×H small matmuls per layer, which also improves throughput.

evidence.finding: RoPE encodes absolute position by rotation with explicit relative dependency; now standard in Llama/OLMo/SmolLM and the modded-nanoGPT recipes.

evidence.source: Wortsman et al., Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities
evidence.finding: qk-layernorm prevents attention-logit growth and enables stable training across ~3 orders of magnitude of LR, shown with small models.
QK-norm (with other norm changes) improved training stability and loss in OLMo 2.

expected_effect: ≈ −0.02 to −0.05 nats; a higher usable peak LR; a 10–25% throughput gain from fusing, which buys time headroom for other changes.
applicability: Pure architecture change with a slight parameter decrease (−32K). The ingredients are standard at every scale, including the 124M speedrun. Fusing uses SDPA, which is available in fp32 on an L4.
risks: The RoPE implementation must use correct pairing and cache cos/sin for T≤128. QK-norm removes implicit temperature learning; add a learnable gain or keep the default scale. Some code logs attention_values/embedding tensors, so keep attrs or guard them.
implementation: MultiHeadAttention.__init__: self.qkv=nn.Linear(C,3C,bias=False); self.proj=nn.Linear(C,C); hd=C//H; inv=1/(10000**(torch.arange(0,hd,2)/hd)); t=torch.arange(block_size); f=torch.outer(t,inv); register_buffer cos=f.cos(), sin=f.sin(). forward: q,k,v=self.qkv(x).view(B,T,3,H,hd).unbind(2); q,k=F.rms_norm(q,(hd,)),F.rms_norm(k,(hd,)); rotate: x1,x2=x[...,::2]... or half-split: y=cat(x1*cos-x2*sin, x1*sin+x2*cos); transpose to (B,H,T,hd); y=F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=True); proj. Keep Head class unused or delete. In forward_body: x=tok_emb (no pos_emb); keep position_embedding_table out of model_init.

name: ReLU² (or param-matched SwiGLU) MLP
proposal: Option A (modded-nanoGPT style): same shapes, activation F.relu(x).square(), bias=False, zero-init the output projection. Option B: SwiGLU with hidden = 683 (≈ 8/3·C, param-matched): w2(silu(w1 x) * w3 x).
mechanism: Squared ReLU and gated units give sharper, sparser feature selection and a better loss per FLOP than GELU in language-model FFNs. Both are drop-ins with equal parameter count.

evidence.finding: Squared-ReLU is one of the two modifications responsible for most of Primer's gains; it cuts training cost up to 4x combined with dconv, and the benefit is robust across scales and codebases.
GEGLU/SwiGLU give the best perplexities vs ReLU/GELU FFNs at matched params/compute.

applicability: Parameter-neutral and cheap. ReLU² is what the current modded-nanoGPT speedrun (small FineWeb models) uses. SwiGLU is used in every Llama-family small model (TinyLlama, SmolLM).
risks: ReLU² can produce larger activations. That is fine with pre-norm, but pair it with zero/small-init output projections. SwiGLU at hidden 683 adds one more matmul and slightly lowers throughput.
implementation: FeedForward: self.fc=nn.Linear(C,4C,bias=False); self.proj=nn.Linear(4C,C,bias=False); init_weights: nn.init.zeros_(self.proj.weight) (or xavier*0.5). forward: h=F.relu(self.fc(x)).square(); self.gelu_activation=h.detach() (keep attr for logging); return self.dropout(self.proj(h)). SwiGLU variant: w1,w3=Linear(C,683), w2=Linear(683,C); return w2(F.silu(w1(x))*w3(x)).

name: Linear decay-to-zero (D2Z) LR schedule
current: Linear warmup 300 steps, then cosine from 2e-3 down to min_lr 2e-6.
proposal: Linear warmup (300 steps, or ~2% of steps), then decay linearly to 0 over the rest (min_lr=0). Optionally, a WSD variant: hold the peak until 70–80% of steps, then decay linearly to 0.
mechanism: Viewing AdamW as an EMA of weight updates, linear D2Z balances early movement away from init against late averaging of gradient noise better than cosine does. Cosine spends too long at low LR and too little at mid LR.

evidence.source: Bergsma et al., Straight to Zero: Why Linearly Decaying the LR to Zero Works Best for LLMs
evidence.finding: Linear D2Z consistently beats cosine (10x decay) across model sizes, batch sizes and datasets. The advantage grows with tokens-per-parameter; 610M at 80 TPP with D2Z beat 200 TPP with 10x decay.

expected_effect: ≈ −0.005 to −0.02 nats. Small but nearly free.
applicability: The current cosine already reaches ~0, so the gain comes only from the shape (more time at mid-range LR). The run's 6.9 TPP is low, and the paper found smaller gains at low TPP. That makes this a low-risk polish that stacks with the other cards.
risks: Minor. If combined with Muon, apply the same multiplier schedule to both parts.
implementation: lr_at_step: warmup unchanged; after warmup: progress=(step-warmup)/(total-warmup) clamped; return min_lr + (lr-min_lr)*(1-progress). Set min_lr=0.0. WSD option: if progress<0.75: return lr; else return lr*(1-(progress-0.75)/0.25).

name: Spend freed wall-clock on depth: deep-thin 8–10 layers (bolder)
current: 6 layers × 256 wide, 4 heads. Only 4.8M non-embedding params, 27% of the total. The run takes 2898 s of a ~3660 s cap.
proposal: After fusing attention (card 2), raise n_layer to 8 (~19.3M params; +1.58M) or 10 if throughput allows, keeping n_embd=256 and n_head=4 (head dim 64).
mechanism: Loss mostly tracks non-embedding capacity. Here the lm_head/embedding (12.9M) dominates FLOPs, so each extra block costs only ~5% more compute yet adds ~33% more non-embedding capacity per two layers. At sub-billion scale, depth beats width.

evidence.source: Liu et al., MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter LMs
evidence.finding: At 125M/350M, deep-and-thin architectures (e.g. 30 layers instead of 12) with embedding sharing gave a +2.7%/4.3% accuracy boost over prior same-size models.

expected_effect: ≈ −0.02 to −0.05 nats if the run stays within the time cap.
applicability: The parameter cap (26.5M) allows up to ~12 layers. The binding constraint is time. The current per-head loop wastes throughput, and fusing likely recovers enough for +2 to +4 layers in fp32 on an L4.
risks: Wall-clock overrun (check tok/s in a screen run first). The evidence is at 125M+, larger than here. The model is already under-trained at 6.9 TPP, so returns from extra depth may be smaller.
implementation: Hyperparameter change: n_layer=8 (try 10 if tok/s ≥ ~40k after card 2). Keep everything else fixed. Estimated time = 122.88M / measured tok/s; must be < ~3500 s including eval.
